verses.1: Al-Mizan says the opening glorification prepares for the chapter's coming censure of believers who say what they do not do and its warning of God's displeasure and of hearts being turned aside. The universal glorification establishes that the speaker is the Mighty and Wise.
verses.2: Al-Mizan reads the interrogative as censure addressed to genuine believers, not an allusion to hypocrites. It rejects the claim that believers are too exalted to be reproved: Qur'anic rebukes around Uhud, al-Ahzab, Hunayn, Hudaybiyya, Tabuk, spending, and similar matters were instruments of their gradual divine formation into the righteous. The general wording censures every contradiction of speech and action, broken promise, and breached covenant as a manifestation of outward and inward contradiction, hence hypocrisy. Yet this chapter's context specifies the immediate case: Muslims who promised steadfastness in battle, then fled; delayed after agreeing to set out; or withheld promised provision for fighting.
verses.3: Al-Mizan defines maqt as extreme hatred and makes the verse the reason for the preceding rebuke: speaking contrary to action is hypocrisy. It distinguishes that from merely failing to carry out what one says. The latter springs from weak purpose, resolve, and determination, not necessarily hypocrisy, but is still a vice opposed to felicity. Since human happiness rests on freely performed good deeds and noble traits, and these depend upon firm resolve, a person whose deeds repeatedly fail his words cannot hope for that felicity.
verses.4: Al-Mizan explains saff as an even, straight line, used here as the fighters' state, and bunyan marsus as a structure compacted or strengthened with lead so that destructive force cannot penetrate it. The verse therefore praises those who fight in God's way while holding their ordered ranks. It also supplies the positive counterpart to the earlier censure: if God loves fighters who keep their positions and do not flee, He hates those who promised resolve and then broke that promise on reaching battle.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan reads Moses' complaint as a warning to Muslims not knowingly to hurt the Prophet Muhammad in word or deed, lest they incur the fate of Israel: the turning aside of hearts. The harm to Moses was not simply disobedience, for God's clearing him of it in (33:69) shows that it was slander and imputing shameful things to him; (33:53) similarly illustrates hurtful speech and conduct toward Muhammad. Zaygh is departure from integrity and truth toward falsehood.

God's making their hearts turn aside is not primary misguidance. Their own immoral deviation first made them turn away from mercy and guidance; as requital, God withheld mercy and discontinued guidance, confirming and fixing that deviation in their hearts. The ending that God does not guide transgressors states this reason. Al-Mizan therefore rejects the objection that attributing such misguidance to God would be unjust, since injustice would arise only if it were initial rather than retributive. It also rejects the claim that the reading is pointless once they have strayed: the person's deviation and disbelief arise from his evil, whereas God's distinct act is the consequential establishment and sealing of that deviation.
verses.6:
Al-Mizan presents Jesus' speech as the summary of his mission: he is only God's messenger, confirming the Torah and announcing the messenger after him, Ahmad. His confirmation means that his call did not contradict the Torah's religion or laws, except for a small abrogated part; abrogation ends a law's term rather than proving it false. Jesus therefore forms the intermediate link: he maintains the prior law while announcing the more complete mission that will finish its path.

Glad tidings must concern a good that benefits those addressed. The later message is thus more advanced, comprehensive, and conducive to happiness in this life and the next, while divine calls remain one in essence. Al-Mizan finds this completion especially in Islam's tawhid, the principle underlying all its teachings, and in practical regulations that order every significant individual and social act toward felicity. It cites (7:157) and (48:29) as evidence that the Messenger was written of in the Torah and Injil. Although (61:6) itself says Jesus announced him without itself proving the announcement was recorded in Jesus' book, those verses do.

The name Ahmad is treated as a real name by which Muhammad was known, supported in the passage by verses of Hassan and Abu Talib and by the acceptance of Jewish and Christian scholars who heard these Qur'anic claims. The absence of the prophecy from present Gospels does not impair the Qur'an's proof; the passage refers back to an earlier discussion of their transmission and reliability. When Ahmad came with the clear arguments, including the Qur'an, other signs, and the prior good news, the Children of Israel, or they together with others, called it clear magic. A reported alternative reading calls him a clear magician. The suggestion that the pronoun refers to Jesus is rejected by the context.
verses.7: Al-Mizan reads the rhetorical question as condemnatory rebuttal of the previous charge that the Prophet's message is clear magic. Islam is the religion to which the Messenger calls: submission to what God wills in belief and action, a submission required by God's divinity. To call that religion false or not from God is therefore to forge a lie against Him. The clause that the person is being invited to Islam is itself the proof of the fabrication. Since injustice grows with the greatness of the one wronged, fabricating against God is the greatest injustice, and God does not guide those who commit it.
verses.8: Al-Mizan explains God's light as His religion, and extinguishing it as abolishing its rise and radiance by blowing with the mouth. It preserves al-Raghib's distinction from (9:32): there the construction expresses desiring the extinguishing itself, whereas here it expresses desiring the means to it, the blow, though the ultimate aim remains extinguishment. The context is the opponents' charge of magic; by that speech they seek to make God's light seem as weak as a candle and deny that the religion comes from Him. They are mistaken, for Islam cannot be extinguished. God will not guide them to this aim, but will perfect His light and make His religion prevail even while disbelievers detest it.
verses.9: Al-Mizan argues that din al-haqq is primarily a possessive relation, not merely an explanatory one: both truth and falsehood have a religion proper to them, and God, the Truth Most High, sent the religion proper to truth. Making it prevail means aiding it to triumph over every followed path other than God's path, Islam. The verse explains God's promise to perfect His light in (61:8): that light on earth is the guidance and religion of truth sent with the Messenger, and it will overcome all religions despite the idolaters' aversion. The same identification of the religion of truth with God's light is corroborated by (24:35).
verses.10: Al-Mizan takes the interrogative as an imperative invitation. Tijara is investment of capital for profit, and here faith in God and His Messenger together with striving in God's way are the transaction: the human soul is the capital and deliverance from painful punishment its profit. The comparison is (9:111), where believers' persons and property are bought for the Garden. The language magnifies the transaction and the otherwise inestimable horror from which it saves. That salvation is specifically forgiveness and Paradise, as (61:12) explains; divine help and near victory in (61:13) are a distinct, additional promise and must not be folded into the promised deliverance.
verses.11: Al-Mizan reads this as the explanation of the transaction proposed in the preceding verse: it consists of faith in God and His Messenger and striving with property and life. Faith in the Messenger is inseparable from faith in God because faith requires obedience to the Messenger's instruction; separating God from His messengers is the disbelief described in (4:150) and (4:151). The statement that this is better applies to people of knowledge, whose deeds count for something; alternatively, it says that those possessing knowledge and understanding would recognize its goodness.
verses.12: Al-Mizan supplies the implicit conditional: if believers have faith and strive with property and life, God forgives their sins and admits them to gardens and goodly dwellings of perpetuity. The forgiveness is unrestricted, hence covers all sins; entry into an eternal paradise while faults remained would be incoherent, and the stability and permanence of its dwellings confirms that comprehensive forgiveness. The verse contrasts the small, perishable soul expended in God's path with the eternal Garden, strengthening resolve to choose permanence over extinction. This is the mighty achievement.
verses.13: Al-Mizan takes ukhra, another, as standing for an omitted blessing or characteristic, whose content is divine help and a near, anticipated victory. It is conjoined to the preceding promises, and the command to give good news completes the whole sequence of faith, striving, forgiveness, Paradise, and this additional worldly blessing. In light of (9:111), the good news is not confined to help and victory but embraces all promised recompense, worldly and otherworldly. This contextual reading is preferred over other proposed analyses; the suggestion that the final command begins a new narrative remains possible.
verses.14:
Al-Mizan makes being helpers of God a settled, constant characteristic flowing from the transaction of investing life and wealth in faith and struggle. Helping God means helping His Prophet on the path by which he calls to God with certainty, not supplying a divine lack. The parallel with Jesus' question and the disciples' reply proves the point: their help to God was help to Jesus in his monotheistic, sincere worship and mission. For Muhammad's community it is therefore belief in him, obedience to his commands and prohibitions, decisive speech, sincere action, and striving to propagate the mission and raise the truth.

The outcome of Jesus' appeal also prefigures this community. Israel divided into believers and disbelievers; God aided the believers over their enemies after they had been disregarded and downtrodden. If Muhammad's believers answer his call, God will similarly aid them to become uppermost. The wording that puts God in the Prophet's place magnifies the Prophet's affair and shows divine favor toward him. Al-Mizan directs readers to the fuller account beginning at (3:52).
